lessons.title: What MACD Actually Measures
lessons.summary: Read the MACD line, signal line and histogram as what they really are — a speed reading and an acceleration reading of price — rather than as buy and sell lights.
lessons.html:
Most traders meet MACD as a pair of wiggly lines under the chart and a rule somebody posted online: buy when the blue line crosses above the orange one, sell when it crosses back. They try it, it works brilliantly on the three examples in the video, and then it quietly bleeds their account in the following month. The usual conclusion is that MACD "doesn't work".

MACD works perfectly. It does exactly what its arithmetic says it does, every single candle, without fail. The problem is that very few people are told what that arithmetic is. Once you know, the indicator stops being a set of traffic lights and becomes something far more useful: an honest measuring instrument for the speed of a trend and whether that speed is rising or falling.

This lesson builds that understanding from the ground up. There are no trade setups here yet. By the end, you should be able to look at any MACD pane and say, in plain English, what price has been doing — and, just as importantly, what MACD cannot possibly tell you.

Three numbers, one idea

MACD stands for Moving Average Convergence Divergence. It was developed by Gerald Appel in the late 1970s, and the histogram was added later by Thomas Aspray. Strip away the name and it is three numbers, recalculated on every candle:

  1. The MACD line. The 12-period exponential moving average (EMA) of the closing price, minus the 26-period EMA. That is all. When the fast average is above the slow one, the MACD line is positive. When it is below, the line is negative.
  2. The signal line. A 9-period EMA of the MACD line itself — an average of the difference.
  3. The histogram. The MACD line minus the signal line, drawn as bars.

The settings you see printed as "MACD (12, 26, 9)" are simply those three periods. Every MACD chart in this course uses them, because they are what almost every platform loads by default. Lesson 3 deals with whether changing them helps (mostly, it does not).

The name tells you the idea. The two averages converge when they move towards each other and diverge when they spread apart. The MACD line is a single number that records the gap between them.

Look at the chart above slowly. The MACD pane is not adding information that the price pane does not contain. It is re-plotting one feature of the price pane — the distance between two averages — so that your eye can read it without squinting at two lines that are close together.

KEY POINT

The MACD line is the 12 EMA minus the 26 EMA. Nothing more mysterious is going on.

The MACD line is a speedometer

Why would the gap between a fast and a slow average matter? Because of lag. An EMA trails behind price, and a slower EMA trails further. In a steady trend, the 12 EMA sits a little behind price and the 26 EMA sits further behind. The faster price is travelling, the further behind both averages fall, and the wider the gap between them becomes.

So the MACD line is, in effect, a speedometer for the trend:

  • A large positive value means price has been rising quickly over the last few weeks of candles.
  • A small positive value means price has been rising slowly, or has stopped rising recently.
  • Zero means the fast and slow averages agree — price has, on balance, gone nowhere over the lookback.
  • Negative values are the same story for falling prices.

That framing immediately clears up a common confusion. A rising MACD line does not mean price is rising. It means price is rising faster than it was. A falling MACD line that is still above zero does not mean price is falling. It means the uptrend is losing speed. Price can make new highs while the MACD line falls, simply because each new high arrived more slowly than the last. Lesson 6 turns that observation into a tool called divergence.

There is a simple piece of arithmetic behind this, and it is worth knowing because it removes all the mystery. An EMA lags a steady trend by roughly half its period. The 12 EMA trails by about 5.5 candles and the 26 EMA by about 12.5. In a perfectly steady trend moving k pips per candle, the gap between them settles at roughly 7 × k. A pair climbing a steady 3 pips per candle will show a MACD line of about +21 pips. Speed it up to 5 pips per candle and the reading settles near +35. The MACD line really is a speed reading, measured in pips.

The signal line and histogram: acceleration

If the MACD line is speed, the histogram is acceleration.

The signal line is an average of the MACD line over the last nine candles. Comparing the MACD line with its own recent average tells you whether speed is currently above or below what it has been lately:

  • Histogram bars above zero and growing: the trend is speeding up.
  • Histogram bars above zero but shrinking: still faster than the recent average, but the increase is fading.
  • Histogram crossing below zero: speed has dropped below its recent average. Something is slowing.

The histogram crossing zero is exactly the same event as the famous "MACD crosses the signal line". They are one event drawn two ways. When you hear a trader talk about a "bullish crossover", they mean the histogram has turned from red to green.

A useful mental picture: you are a passenger in a car. The speedometer is the MACD line. The feeling of being pressed back into your seat is the histogram. You can be travelling at 70 miles an hour (high MACD) with no feeling of acceleration at all (histogram near zero). You can be travelling slowly but feel a strong push (low MACD, growing histogram) as the driver puts their foot down. Neither reading tells you where the car will be in ten minutes.

COMMON MISTAKE

Reading red histogram bars as "bearish". Red bars above a positive MACD line mean an uptrend is slowing down. Slowing is not reversing — most healthy uptrends slow down several times before they end.

What MACD cannot tell you

An honest instrument has an honest specification. MACD measures the relationship between two averages of past closing prices. That means there are things it simply cannot see.

It cannot see levels. MACD has no idea that price is sitting on a major support zone, a prior swing high or a round number. It will happily show strong upward momentum straight into resistance. Levels come from the price chart.

It cannot see the future. Every input is a past close. When MACD turns, it is because price has already turned. That is not a flaw to be fixed with clever settings; it is the definition of an average. Lesson 2 measures exactly how much this lag costs.

It does not know about ranges. In a sideways market, the two averages wind around each other and the MACD line wanders back and forth across zero, producing a stream of crossovers that mean almost nothing. Lesson 8 is devoted to this.

Its values are not comparable across markets. Because the MACD line is measured in price units, a reading of +20 on EUR/USD hourly and +20 on USD/JPY daily mean completely different things. The numbers on the axis matter far less than the shape: rising or falling, above or below zero, growing or shrinking bars.

Reading a MACD pane in four questions

Before any of the strategies later in this course, train your eye with four questions. Ask them, in this order, every time you look at a MACD pane:

  1. Is the MACD line above or below zero? This tells you whether the 12 EMA is above or below the 26 EMA — a broad description of which side has been in control recently.
  2. Is the MACD line rising or falling? This tells you whether the trend's speed is increasing or decreasing.
  3. Are the histogram bars growing or shrinking? This tells you whether that change in speed is itself gaining or losing force.
  4. Does the price chart agree? Swing highs and lows, support and resistance, and the slope of price always have the final word.

Work through the four charts in this lesson using those questions. You will find you can describe each one in a sentence: "fast uptrend, now slowing", "trend paused then accelerated", "no trend at all". That sentence is what MACD is for. Everything else in this course builds on it.

Going deeper

The histogram is a rate of change of a rate of change. The MACD line approximates the first derivative of a smoothed price — its slope. The signal line is that slope smoothed again over nine candles, which lags it by roughly four candles. So the histogram (MACD minus signal) is approximately four times the recent change in the MACD line: a smoothed second derivative. This is why the histogram turns first, the MACD line turns second, and the zero line is crossed last. The order is mechanical, not a market pattern, and you should expect it every time.

Why EMAs and not SMAs. An exponential average weights recent closes more heavily, so it responds faster and does not "drop" an old price off the end of the window. With simple averages, a big candle leaving the window can move the indicator even when nothing happens today. EMA-based MACD avoids that artefact, which is one reason the default has survived for decades.

Volatility scaling. Because MACD is in price units, a quiet market produces small readings and a volatile market large ones. Some traders divide MACD by price, or by the average true range, to make readings comparable across markets — the "percentage price oscillator" is the first of those. For the discretionary methods in this course you do not need any of that, because every decision is made relative to the same chart's recent history: is the line higher or lower than before, above or below zero, are the bars growing or shrinking?

Start-up distortion. An EMA needs history to settle. The first few dozen candles of any MACD calculation are unreliable, because the averages were seeded on a single price. Platforms handle this by loading plenty of history; it only matters if you are building the indicator yourself or testing on short data sets.

Summary

  • The MACD line is the 12 EMA minus the 26 EMA — the gap between a fast and a slow average.
  • Read the line as speed: positive and rising means an uptrend that is speeding up; positive and falling means an uptrend that is slowing.
  • The signal line is a 9-period average of the MACD line; the histogram is the difference, and reads as acceleration.
  • "Signal line crossover" and "histogram changes colour" are the same event.
  • MACD cannot see levels, cannot see the future, and produces meaningless crossovers in ranges. Price structure has the final word.

quiz.q: What does the MACD line measure?
options: The difference between the 12 EMA and the 26 EMA of price
The number of up candles minus down candles
The average of the last 9 closes
quiz.why: MACD line = 12 EMA minus 26 EMA. It contains no volume or candle-count information.

quiz.q: The MACD line is above zero but falling. Which description is correct?
quiz.why: Above zero means the fast EMA is still above the slow EMA; falling means the gap is narrowing — the uptrend is slowing. Price can still be rising.

quiz.q: A trader says 'the MACD just crossed its signal line to the upside'. What does the histogram show at that moment?
options: It crosses from below zero to above zero
It turns from green to red
quiz.why: The histogram is MACD minus signal, so a bullish signal-line cross is the histogram moving from negative to positive.

quiz.q: In a steady trend rising 4 pips per candle, roughly where will the MACD line settle with default settings?
quiz.why: The 26 EMA lags about 7 candles more than the 12 EMA, so the gap settles near 7 × 4 = 28 pips. This shows the line is a speed reading.

quiz.q: Price is pressing into a major resistance zone and MACD shows strong upward momentum. What does MACD tell you about the resistance?
options: It will break, because momentum is strong
It will hold, because MACD is overbought
Nothing — MACD cannot see price levels
It will break only if the histogram is green
quiz.why: MACD is built from averages of closes and has no knowledge of levels. Levels come from the price chart.

lessons.title: Why Crossovers Lag — and What It Costs
lessons.summary: Measure the delay built into every MACD crossover, count its cost in pips and stop distance, and recognise the situations where that cost wipes out the trade.
lessons.html:
The most popular MACD rule in the world is the signal-line crossover: buy when the MACD line crosses above its signal line, sell when it crosses below. It is simple, it is mechanical, and on a chart of a big trend it looks spectacular. The arrows land near the bottom of every rally and near the top of every decline.

Look closer and they do not land near the bottom. They land after it. Every single time. That is not bad luck and it is not a setting you have got wrong. It is built into the arithmetic, and once you understand the arithmetic you can put a number on it — and decide when the price of being late is worth paying.

This lesson does that. You will see exactly where the delay comes from, measure it on charts, and learn the three ways it costs you money: a worse entry, a wider stop, and a later exit.

The order of events is fixed

Lesson 1 showed that the MACD line measures speed and the histogram measures acceleration. When a downtrend turns into an uptrend, those readings have to change in a fixed order:

  1. The histogram bottoms first. The decline stops accelerating. Price is still falling, just not faster than before.
  2. The histogram crosses zero. This is the signal-line crossover. The decline has slowed enough that the MACD line is now rising faster than its own nine-candle average. Price has usually already made its low.
  3. The MACD line crosses zero. The 12 EMA finally climbs back above the 26 EMA. By now price has typically travelled a good distance off the low.

This sequence is mechanical. It happens in every reversal on every chart. The only thing that changes is how far apart the three events are, and that depends on how the reversal unfolds.

Notice the trade-off in that chart, because it runs through the whole of this course. The earliest event, the histogram turning, was spectacularly early: price kept falling for another 17 candles. Anyone who bought that "momentum shift" sat through nearly 100 pips of loss. The latest event, the zero-line cross, was reliable — by then the trend had clearly changed — but it gave away most of the first leg of the rally. The signal-line cross sat in between.

There is no setting that removes this trade-off. Faster settings move all three events earlier and make each one less reliable. Slower settings do the reverse. Lesson 3 returns to this.

KEY POINT

MACD events always arrive in the same order — histogram, signal cross, zero cross — and each later event is more reliable and more expensive.

Where the lag comes from

The MACD line is built from two exponential averages. An EMA of period N lags a steady trend by roughly (N − 1) ÷ 2 candles: about 5.5 candles for the 12 EMA and 12.5 for the 26 EMA. The signal line is then a 9-period average of that difference, adding roughly another four candles of delay to anything measured against it.

In practice that means a signal-line crossover cannot happen until price has moved far enough, for long enough, to drag the 12 EMA's slope above its recent average. On a sharp V-shaped low, that happens quickly — one to three candles. On a slow, rounded low, where price drifts sideways for a while before rising, it can take ten candles or more, because nothing in the averages changes until price actually starts moving.

That is the first counter-intuitive fact about crossovers: they are most punctual in the violent reversals you would have spotted anyway, and least punctual in the slow turns where you most want help.

Cost one: the worse entry

The obvious cost is price. If the crossover arrives 16 pips above the low, you buy 16 pips higher than the low. That sounds small — and on the chart above, it was small. But that is a 60-pip-per-hour V bottom. On the rounded turns that make up most of the market, the gap is routinely larger, and it is paid on every trade.

Cost two: the wider stop

The less obvious cost is risk. Where does the stop go on a crossover buy? The only structural place is below the low that was just made. Every pip the crossover arrives late is a pip added to the distance between your entry and your stop.

Run the numbers with illustrative values. A trader risks 1% of the account per trade. If the stop is 20 pips away, they can trade a position worth 0.05% of the account per pip. If lag pushes the stop to 40 pips, the same 1% risk buys half the position. The trade can go exactly the same way and pay half as much. Lag does not just cost pips; it shrinks size.

Cost three: the later exit

Traders who buy on crossovers usually sell on crossovers, and the exit lags just as badly as the entry. The result on a whole trend is a chain of costs: in late, out late, and — worst of all — shaken out in the middle.

The middle of that chart is where crossover systems really hurt. The pullback between the two rallies was an ordinary, healthy correction — the kind Lesson 7 teaches you to buy. The crossover system sold it instead, then bought back higher once the trend resumed. Nothing went wrong; the indicator did exactly what its maths dictates. It simply cannot tell the difference between a pullback and a reversal, because both look like "speed falling".

When the lag eats the whole move

On a big trend, late entries and late exits still leave something on the table for you. The dangerous case is the small move. If the swing is only slightly larger than the crossover's built-in delay, the signal arrives right where the move ends.

This is the losing trade every crossover trader knows. The bounce was real, the crossover was real, and the trade was still a loss, because by the time the signal was confirmed the bounce was nearly finished. Note what the chart was saying all along: the MACD line never got near zero. It was a pause in a downtrend, not a new uptrend. Lesson 4 turns that observation into a filter that would have skipped this trade.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a crossover as a timing signal on its own. On small swings the delay is a large fraction of the move, so the signal arrives after most of the opportunity has gone and the stop must be wide.

Practice drill

Use what you have learned so far. The chart below stops at the moment a bullish crossover prints. Decide before you press reveal.

The answer is in the reveal, but think about how you would have worked it out. Three questions do most of the work: how far is the stop, how much room is left, and is the trend gaining or losing speed? A crossover answers none of them.

Going deeper

Quantifying the delay. You can estimate the lag of a crossover on any chart without software. Count the candles between a clear swing low and the bullish signal-line cross that followed. Do this for the last 20 swings on your chosen market and timeframe and note the average delay and its spread. Then measure the typical swing size in pips. If the average delay costs more than about a third of the typical swing, a stand-alone crossover approach is structurally weak on that market — before spreads.

The rounded-turn problem. An EMA only changes slope when new closes differ from its current value. In a slow, flat bottom, closes hover around the averages, so nothing in the MACD changes until the breakout candle arrives. On these turns the crossover often prints on the same candle as a simple break of the range high — and the range high was the better reference, because it also tells you where the stop belongs.

Why exits hurt more than entries. Entries are optional; you can skip a late one. A crossover exit rule is compulsory, and it fires on every pullback big enough to slow the trend. In strongly trending markets a large share of the profit comes from staying in through those pullbacks. Many experienced traders therefore use MACD for context and entry timing but manage exits with structure — a close beyond the last higher low, for example — rather than with the opposite crossover.

Expectancy, illustratively. Imagine two hypothetical systems with identical direction calls. System A enters 10 pips after the turn, System B 30 pips after. Average stop distance rises from 25 to 45 pips. If both risk 1% per trade, System B trades about 44% smaller on every position, and its targets are 20 pips closer to wherever the move eventually ends. The numbers are invented; the shape of the problem is not. Lateness compounds through position size.

Summary

  • MACD events arrive in a fixed order: histogram turns, signal line crosses, zero line crosses — each later event more reliable and more expensive.
  • Lag comes from the averages themselves; no setting removes it, only trades it for noise.
  • Lag costs you three ways: a worse entry, a wider stop (and so a smaller position at fixed risk), and a later exit.
  • Crossover exits shake you out of healthy pullbacks and force you to re-enter higher.
  • On small swings the delay can consume the whole move. A crossover alone is not a strategy.

quiz.q: In a reversal from downtrend to uptrend, which MACD event happens first?
options: Histogram stops falling and turns up
They happen at the same time
quiz.why: The histogram measures acceleration, so it turns as soon as the decline stops speeding up — before the signal cross and well before the zero cross.

quiz.q: Why does a late crossover entry usually mean a smaller position for the same 1% account risk?
options: The stop under the swing low is further away, so fewer units fit inside the same risk
MACD signals require smaller lots by convention
quiz.why: Position size is risk divided by stop distance. A later entry widens the stop distance, so the same risk buys fewer units.

quiz.q: On which type of turn does a signal-line cross typically arrive most promptly?
options: A gap at the weekly open
quiz.why: In a V reversal, the MACD's speed reading changes abruptly, so the cross arrives within a few candles. Slow, rounded turns delay it.

quiz.q: In the 'In late, out early, back in higher' chart, what caused the mid-trend loss of position?
options: A bearish cross during an ordinary pullback
quiz.why: A healthy pullback slows the trend enough to trigger a bearish cross. The system sold and then bought back higher when the trend resumed.

quiz.q: A bullish cross prints 40 pips above the swing low on a market whose typical swing is 60 pips. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing — a cross is a cross
The delay has consumed most of the typical swing, leaving poor reward for a wide stop
The histogram is the wrong colour
The MACD settings are too slow for that pair
quiz.why: When lag eats a large fraction of the typical move, the remaining reward is small relative to the stop distance.

quiz.q: Which of these would a crossover-only system be unable to tell apart?
options: An H1 chart and an H4 chart
A green and a red candle
quiz.why: Both a pullback and a reversal reduce trend speed, so both trigger the opposite crossover. Only price structure separates them.

lessons.title: Settings, Timeframes and the Myths
lessons.summary: Choose MACD settings for sound reasons, use timeframe rather than parameters to change what MACD sees, and spot the settings myths that cost traders months.
lessons.html:
Sooner or later every MACD user goes looking for better settings. Someone on a forum swears by 5, 35, 5. A course sells "the institutional MACD" with numbers that turn out to be 8, 17, 9. A backtest shows that 10, 23, 7 would have made a fortune on EUR/USD last year. The default 12, 26, 9 starts to look old-fashioned.

This lesson will save you that search. Changing the settings does not change what MACD is. It only moves you along one line — earlier and noisier at one end, later and calmer at the other — and you already have better ways to move along that line. By the end you will know why the defaults are fine, what actually changes when you change them, and why the timeframe you choose matters far more than the numbers you type in.

What the three numbers do

Recall the definition from Lesson 1. In MACD (12, 26, 9):

  • 12 is the period of the fast EMA.
  • 26 is the period of the slow EMA.
  • 9 is the period of the signal line, an EMA of the MACD line.

Shorten the first two and the averages hug price more tightly. The MACD line responds sooner to changes in speed, and it also responds to smaller wiggles that do not matter. Lengthen them and the line becomes smoother, slower and quieter. Shorten the third and the signal line chases the MACD line more closely, producing more crossovers. Lengthen it and crossovers become rarer and later.

That is the entire menu. Every setting you will ever see online is a point on the same trade-off between responsiveness and reliability. There is no combination that is both earlier and cleaner, because both properties come from the same averaging.

KEY POINT

Every MACD setting is a trade between lag and noise. No setting removes lag without adding noise.

You already have three speeds built in

Before reaching for new numbers, notice that the standard MACD already offers three different speeds. Lesson 2 showed them as a fixed sequence: histogram first, signal-line cross second, zero-line cross last. Choosing which of those events you act on changes the indicator's speed far more than adjusting a parameter from 12 to 10.

That chart is the whole settings debate in one picture. A trader who found the signal-line crosses too noisy might go looking for slower settings. But the zero line on the default indicator already gives a slower, calmer reading of the same trend. Lessons 4 and 5 build methods around exactly this: the zero line for direction, the histogram for timing.

The timeframe is the real setting

MACD does not know what a candle is. It counts them. A 12-period EMA on an hourly chart averages the last 12 hours; on a four-hour chart it averages the last 48 hours. So changing the timeframe changes what the indicator measures far more dramatically than changing the parameters.

There is a useful rule of thumb here. Each four-hour candle contains four hourly candles, so MACD (12, 26, 9) on the H4 chart sees roughly what MACD (48, 104, 36) would see on the H1 chart. If you find yourself wanting much slower settings on a lower timeframe, what you probably want is the higher timeframe, viewed with its normal settings. You will get a cleaner picture, with candles that carry their own information, rather than a stretched-out average of noise.

Now look at the same kind of pullback through an hourly lens.

Neither chart is wrong. They answer different questions. The higher timeframe tells you which direction you want to trade; the lower timeframe tells you whether the pullback within it is still running or has started to turn. This is the basis of the multi-timeframe approach used later in the course: direction from the higher timeframe, timing from the lower one, and the standard settings on both.

COMMON MISTAKE

Changing MACD settings to stop the lower-timeframe indicator from "disagreeing" with the higher timeframe. The disagreement is the information. A pullback on the higher timeframe is supposed to look like a small downtrend on the lower one.

Five myths, briefly

Myth 1: there is an optimal setting. You can always find settings that would have performed best on a past data set. That tells you about the past data set, not about next month. The more parameters you optimise, and the more finely you tune them, the more you are fitting the noise of that sample. Settings that only work at exactly 11, 24, 8 and fall apart at 12, 26, 9 are not an edge; they are an accident.

Myth 2: faster settings fix the lag. They move every signal earlier — including the false ones. On the chart above, a faster MACD would add crossovers during every small wiggle inside each pullback. You exchange a late signal for an early signal that is wrong more often.

Myth 3: MACD has overbought and oversold levels. It does not. Unlike RSI, which is boxed between 0 and 100, MACD is unbounded and measured in price units. A "high" reading is only high compared with the same market's recent readings. There is no universal level at which MACD is "too high".

Myth 4: some currency pairs need special settings. Volatility differs between pairs, so the size of the readings differs. The shape of the readings — rising, falling, above or below zero — means the same thing everywhere. Read shape, not size.

Myth 5: the default settings are arbitrary. They are conventional, which is a different thing. Because almost every platform loads 12, 26, 9, almost every trader looking at MACD is looking at the same picture. That does not make it magic, but it does mean you are reading the same instrument as everyone else, and your observations, notes and backtests transfer between platforms without translation.

MACD reacts to size, not significance

One last point about what the arithmetic does, because it explains a lot of strange MACD behaviour. Because the indicator is built from averages of closes, one enormous candle has an enormous effect on it. A single spike on a data release can produce the largest MACD reading on the chart, even if price gives the whole move back within a day.

The practical rule: treat MACD readings formed by one or two outsized candles with suspicion. Wait for the indicator to reflect a run of candles rather than a single event, and let the price chart — does the breakout hold? does the next pullback stay above the spike's base? — decide whether the move was real.

Going deeper

Lag, quantified. An EMA with period N has a smoothing constant of 2 ÷ (N + 1) and an average lag of about (N − 1) ÷ 2 bars on a steady trend. Halving the fast and slow periods roughly halves the lag of the MACD line — and roughly doubles its sensitivity to single-bar noise. If you test alternative settings, test whole families (for example 8/17/9, 12/26/9 and 19/39/9) and look for broadly similar behaviour across them. Robust ideas survive nearby settings; fragile ones do not.

Choosing a timeframe pair. A ratio of about four to six between timeframes works well: D1 with H4, H4 with H1, H1 with M15. Closer than that and the two charts show nearly the same thing; further apart and the lower timeframe's swings are too small to matter to the higher one.

When a non-default setting is defensible. If you trade a market with very different session structure — one that is only active for a few hours a day, for example — the number of candles per meaningful swing may genuinely differ. The right test is to count candles in typical swings, not to optimise for profit. If the typical swing on your chart lasts 30 candles, a slow EMA of 26 sits sensibly inside it. If typical swings last 8 candles, consider a lower timeframe rather than shorter settings, so each swing contains more candles.

Testing honestly. If you must test settings, split your data. Choose settings on the first half, then run them unchanged on the second half you have not looked at. If performance collapses out of sample, the settings were fitted to noise. Write the result down either way; most traders only remember the tests that worked.

Summary

  • The three numbers set the fast EMA, slow EMA and signal line. Every combination trades lag against noise.
  • The default MACD already offers three speeds: histogram, signal-line cross and zero-line cross. Choose the event before you change the numbers.
  • Timeframe changes MACD far more than settings. H4 with default settings is roughly H1 with settings four times longer — and cleaner.
  • A lower-timeframe MACD disagreeing with a higher-timeframe one is information, not a fault.
  • MACD has no overbought or oversold levels, and single large candles can dominate it.

quiz.q: What happens if you shorten the fast and slow periods of MACD?
options: Signals arrive earlier and the indicator becomes noisier
Signals arrive earlier and become more reliable
The indicator gains overbought and oversold levels
quiz.why: Shorter averages respond sooner but also respond to small wiggles. Earlier always comes with noisier.

quiz.q: Default MACD on H4 sees roughly the same history as which setting on H1?
quiz.why: Each H4 candle contains four H1 candles, so multiply each period by four.

quiz.q: In the 'One trend, eight crosses' chart, which reading gave the calmest picture of the trend?
options: The MACD line relative to zero
quiz.why: The MACD line stayed above zero throughout, while the signal line produced eight crossovers.

quiz.q: The H1 MACD is below zero while the H4 MACD is comfortably above zero. What is the most sensible reading?
options: The indicator is broken on one timeframe
A pullback within a higher-timeframe uptrend
A confirmed downtrend on both timeframes
Change the H1 settings until they agree
quiz.why: A higher-timeframe pullback naturally appears as a small downtrend on the lower timeframe. The disagreement is information.

quiz.q: A MACD reading of +0.0040 on EUR/USD — is the market overbought?
options: No, MACD has no fixed overbought level; it is unbounded and in price units
Yes, if the histogram is green
quiz.why: MACD is not bounded like RSI. A reading is only high or low relative to the same market's recent history.

quiz.q: A single 80-pip news candle produces the largest MACD reading on the chart. How should you treat it?
options: As the strongest buy signal on the chart
With suspicion until price shows follow-through
As a reason to change settings
quiz.why: MACD reacts to candle size, not significance. Let price confirm whether the move holds.

lessons.title: The Zero Line as a Trend Filter
lessons.summary: Use the MACD zero line to decide which direction you are allowed to trade, ignore every crossover that fights it, and know the two situations where the filter itself goes wrong.
lessons.html:
Lesson 2 ended with a losing trade: a bullish crossover that fired in the middle of a downtrend, bought a bounce that was already ending and was stopped out. The chart had been telling the truth all along. The MACD line never got near zero. The bounce was a pause, not a new trend.

That observation is the most useful thing you can do with MACD, and almost nobody uses it properly. The zero line is not a signal. It is a filter — a way of deciding, before you look for any entry at all, which side of the market you are allowed to be on. This lesson shows you how to use it, how much bad trading it removes, and where its own lag will still catch you out.

What the zero line really says

The MACD line is the 12 EMA minus the 26 EMA. So the MACD line is above zero exactly when the 12 EMA is above the 26 EMA, and below zero exactly when it is below. That gives the zero line a simple meaning:

  • Above zero: over the last few weeks of candles, recent prices have been higher than older prices. Buyers have had the better of it.
  • Below zero: recent prices have been lower than older prices. Sellers have had the better of it.

That is a crude definition of trend, but crude is what you want from a filter. It does not need to be clever. It needs to be consistent, and it needs to stop you doing the most expensive thing a short-term trader does: fighting the prevailing direction because a small counter-move looked convincing.

The rule

The zero-line filter is one sentence:

KEY POINT

Trade longs only while the MACD line is above zero. Trade shorts only while it is below zero. Everything else is ignored.

Notice what this rule does not say. It does not say "buy when MACD crosses above zero". The zero cross is not an entry; it is the moment the permission changes. Entries come from elsewhere — the histogram, a pullback to a moving average, a price trigger — and the rest of this course teaches them. The filter's only job is to remove half of them before you even consider them.

What the filter throws away

Here is the same downtrend kind of market that produced Lesson 2's losing trade. Count the bullish crossovers.

Four signals that a crossover trader would have bought are simply not available to a filtered trader. Each of those bounces looked like the start of something at the time. None of them was. That is the filter's value: it does not make you better at reading bounces, it stops you having to.

Now look at the allowed side. The bearish crossovers fired near the top of each bounce, with the MACD line below zero. They still carry all of the lag problems from Lesson 2, but they are pointing in the same direction as the trend, so the trend does some of the work of rescuing a late entry.

A filtered trade, start to finish

The filter becomes useful when you combine it with a sensible entry and a structural stop. Here is the simplest version: a with-trend crossover, taken only because the filter allows it.

Walk through the numbers, which are illustrative. The bullish cross confirmed at 133 pips on the chart's scale. The higher low it formed above sits at 83, so the stop goes at 78, just beneath it: 55 pips of risk. A target at 2R is 110 pips above entry. Risking 1% of the account, a 55-pip stop sets the position size; the target, if reached, returns 2%. The trade worked, but notice the entry was still 50 pips above the low. The filter fixed the direction, not the lag.

When the filter is wrong

A filter built from moving averages has the same weakness as the averages: it is late. There are two situations where that lateness turns into losing trades, and you need to recognise both.

The first is the regime change. After a long trend, the MACD line can stay on the "allowed" side of zero for some time after price has already turned. During that window, the filter keeps permitting trades in a direction that structure has already abandoned.

That trade obeyed the rule and still lost. What would have saved it? Price structure. The decline from the high was fast and deep — over 40% of the whole rally in ten candles — and the bounce failed below the high. Any trend-following trader would call that a warning, and Lesson 9 builds it into the rules. MACD's filter is a minimum condition, never a sufficient one.

The second is the range. When a market goes sideways, the 12 and 26 EMAs wind around each other and the MACD line crosses zero again and again. The filter flips from "longs only" to "shorts only" every few candles, which is another way of saying it has stopped working. Lesson 8 shows how to recognise this early and stand aside.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the zero cross itself as an entry. By the time the 12 EMA crosses the 26 EMA, a new trend is usually well under way and the first pullback has not happened yet. Wait for the pullback.

What to do when the filter switches

The moment the MACD line crosses zero is a change of permission, so treat it as an administrative event rather than a trading one. Three things happen. First, any open position on the old side is reviewed: if its own stop or target has not been reached, the trend reason for holding it has gone, and Lesson 9 makes exiting it a rule. Second, you stop looking for setups on the old side. Third, you start waiting — not trading — on the new side. A fresh trend needs to show you an impulse, a pullback and a reset before the methods in Module 3 have anything to work with. In practice that wait is often ten to thirty candles. It feels like missing the move. It is actually the price of trading only the parts of a move you can define.

Going deeper

Zero line versus a slower moving average. The zero-line filter is equivalent to asking whether the 12 EMA is above the 26 EMA. Many traders use price relative to a 50 or 200 EMA as their trend filter instead. These are close cousins. The MACD version reacts sooner than a 200 EMA filter and is noisier; it sits roughly alongside a 50-period average in speed. If you already use a moving-average filter, adding the MACD zero line on the same timeframe will mostly agree with it and add little. The genuinely useful addition is the higher-timeframe MACD zero line, which Lesson 3 introduced.

A two-timeframe filter. A robust arrangement is: higher-timeframe MACD line above zero sets the direction; trading-timeframe MACD is then used for timing pullbacks within that direction. The trading-timeframe MACD will fall back towards zero during pullbacks, and sometimes slightly below it — Lesson 7 builds its setup around that fall towards zero. What is not allowed is a long while the higher-timeframe MACD is below zero.

Distance from zero. The further the MACD line is from zero, the faster the trend has been. A very large reading after a long run can mean the move is stretched, but MACD has no fixed extreme, so judge this only against the same chart's history. A practical habit: when the MACD line is at its most extreme reading for the last hundred candles, avoid opening new with-trend positions until there has been a pullback that brings it back towards its average.

Measuring what the filter removes. If you keep a trading journal, tag every crossover signal for a month as "with filter" or "against filter" without trading them. Then compare the two groups on a simple measure — how far price moved in the signal's favour before it moved 20 pips against it, for example. Your own data will tell you more about the filter than any book can. Expect the difference to be largest in trending months and smallest in ranging months.

Summary

  • MACD above zero means the 12 EMA is above the 26 EMA; below zero means the reverse. It is a crude but consistent definition of trend.
  • The filter: longs only above zero, shorts only below. Ignore every crossover that fights it.
  • The zero cross is a change of permission, not an entry.
  • The filter removes most counter-trend bounce trades but does not cure lag.
  • It fails at regime changes (it stays open after structure breaks) and in ranges (it flips constantly). Structure overrides it.

quiz.q: The MACD line is below zero and a bullish signal-line crossover prints. What does the zero-line filter say?
options: Ignore it — only shorts are allowed below zero
quiz.why: Below zero the filter permits shorts only. A bullish cross there is a counter-trend signal and is ignored.

quiz.q: What does it mean, in terms of moving averages, when the MACD line is above zero?
options: The 12 EMA is above the 26 EMA
quiz.why: MACD line = 12 EMA − 26 EMA, so it is positive exactly when the 12 EMA is above the 26 EMA.

quiz.q: Why is the MACD zero-line cross a poor entry signal on its own?
options: It arrives late, typically well after the turn and before the first pullback
It is only valid on the daily chart
quiz.why: The 12/26 EMA cross lags the turn substantially. The better entry is usually the first pullback after the regime changes.

quiz.q: In 'The filter is still open — but the trend is not', what warned against the long despite the filter allowing it?
options: A deep, fast drop and a lower high, with a much smaller MACD peak
The MACD line was above zero
quiz.why: Structure had weakened: a fast, deep decline and a lower high. The filter lags structure, and structure wins.

quiz.q: A trader's filter flips between 'longs only' and 'shorts only' six times in forty candles. What is the most likely market condition?
quiz.why: In a range the 12 and 26 EMAs wind around each other, so the MACD line keeps crossing zero and the filter stops being informative.

lessons.title: Reading Histogram Momentum Shifts
lessons.summary: Use the MACD histogram to see a trend's pushes weakening, time the end of a pullback with the histogram hook, and avoid the false alarms that red bars produce in healthy trends.
lessons.html:
The histogram is the part of MACD most traders glance at and least understand. It changes colour often, it moves first, and it looks like it ought to be telling you something urgent. Usually what it is telling you is far more modest than it looks — and occasionally it is the earliest honest warning on the whole chart.

Lesson 1 described the histogram as acceleration: the MACD line's speed reading compared with its own nine-candle average. This lesson turns that description into three practical skills. You will learn to compare the strength of successive pushes, to use the histogram hook to time the end of a pullback, and to stop treating every red bar in an uptrend as an alarm.

Bars are about change, not direction

Start with the single most important fact about the histogram. It does not tell you which way price is going. It tells you whether the MACD line — speed — is rising or falling relative to its recent average.

That means a histogram can be red while price rises, and green while price falls:

  • Red bars in an uptrend mean the uptrend's speed is falling below its recent average. Price may still be rising, just more slowly than it was.
  • Green bars in a downtrend mean the decline is slowing. Price may still be falling.

Once you accept this, a lot of apparently contradictory MACD behaviour stops being confusing.

Anyone who sold that chart because "the histogram turned bearish" sold a trend that had more than a hundred pips left to run. The histogram was accurate: speed was falling. It was the interpretation that was wrong.

KEY POINT

The histogram measures change in speed, not direction. Red bars in an uptrend mean slowing, not falling.

Skill one: comparing pushes

The first useful job for the histogram is comparing the strength of successive pushes in a trend. Each impulse leg in a healthy trend should be accompanied by a cluster of growing bars. If each new push produces smaller bars than the last, the trend is spending more effort for less acceleration.

Read this the right way round. Shrinking histogram peaks across successive pushes do not mean the trend is over; price has made three higher highs and no lower low. They mean the trend is maturing. The practical consequences are defensive: take profits a little sooner, be pickier about new entries, and pay close attention to the next pullback. If it is deeper and faster than the previous ones, the warning is gaining weight. Lesson 6 develops this same idea into divergence, using the MACD line rather than the histogram.

Skill two: the histogram hook

The histogram's most practical use is timing. During a pullback in a trend, the histogram grows on the counter-trend side as the pullback gathers pace. When the pullback starts to lose force, the bars stop growing and begin to shrink. The first bar that is clearly shorter than the one before it is called the hook.

The hook is an early event. It comes before the signal-line cross and well before any zero-line event. That is its value — and, as Lesson 2 warned, its danger. Early signals are cheap but unreliable. So the hook is never an entry on its own. It is a cue to start watching for a price trigger.

The rule for a long is:

  1. The trend filter allows longs (MACD line above zero, or on the higher timeframe as in Lesson 4).
  2. Price has pulled back and the histogram has gone red.
  3. A histogram bar prints that is clearly shorter than the previous red bar — the hook.
  4. A price candle closes above the high of the previous candle. That is the trigger. Enter on its close.
  5. Stop goes below the pullback's low. Target at least twice the risk, or the prior swing high if that is closer and still gives at least 1.5R.

The comparison with the crossover is the point. Both the hook trader and the crossover trader were buying the same pullback in the same trend. The hook trader got in 31 pips cheaper and so needed a stop 23 pips wide rather than more than 50. At the same 1% risk, their position was more than twice the size. That is the real reward for acting earlier.

The price is that early signals fail more often. Here is one that did.

The stop did its job. One loss of 1R against a 2R target is an affordable outcome as long as the method wins often enough over many trades — and you can only find out whether it does by testing it, not by reading about it. What you can do here is look for the clue that would have made you more cautious: a pullback that was steep, fast and unbroken, falling faster per candle than the rally had risen. Pullbacks that look like that deserve a stronger trigger or no trade. Lesson 7 builds that into a full method.

COMMON MISTAKE

Buying the hook without a price trigger. A shrinking red bar only means the decline is slowing. Price can slow and keep falling. Wait for a candle to close above the previous candle's high.

Skill three: ignoring the noise

Most of the time, the histogram is doing nothing worth acting on. In a quiet trend, the bars wobble around zero, flip colour every few candles and mean very little. A useful habit is to ignore the histogram entirely unless one of two things is true: price is in a pullback inside a trend you are allowed to trade (skill two), or you are comparing pushes at a new swing high or low (skill one). Outside those two moments, look at the price chart.

Going deeper

Why the hook comes first. The histogram is MACD minus its 9-period EMA. Because the signal line lags the MACD line by about four candles, the histogram is roughly proportional to how much the MACD line has changed over the last few candles. When the pullback's speed stops increasing, the MACD line's descent flattens and the histogram contracts immediately. The signal cross needs the MACD line to actually rise past its average, which takes several more candles. The zero line needs the 12 EMA to cross the 26 EMA, which takes longer still.

Defining "clearly shorter". Tiny contractions happen constantly, and some will reverse on the next bar. A practical threshold is that the hook bar must be at least 10–15% shorter than the largest bar of the pullback. Alternatively, require two consecutive shorter bars. Both reduce false hooks; both cost a few pips of entry. Write down which you use and do not switch mid-test.

Pullback speed versus impulse speed. The histogram cannot tell you on its own whether a pullback is gentle or violent, because the histogram's swings are naturally large around any turn. Price can. Divide the impulse's size in pips by the number of candles it took, and do the same for the pullback. On the winning chart above the rally covered about 150 pips in 22 candles, roughly 7 pips per candle, and the pullback about 50 pips in 12 candles, roughly 4 per candle: slower than the trend, as a healthy correction should be. On the failed chart the pullback covered about 48 pips in six candles, 8 per candle: faster than the trend it was correcting. Many traders simply skip hook setups when the pullback is travelling faster than the impulse did.

Lower-timeframe histogram for higher-timeframe pullbacks. If the H4 chart is in a pullback, the H1 histogram will produce several hooks inside it. Using the H1 hook as a trigger only when the H4 pullback has reached a sensible area — a moving average or prior structure — is a way to refine entries without changing the logic. Do not take every H1 hook; take the one that occurs where the H4 chart says a pullback should end.

Summary

  • The histogram measures change in the MACD line's speed. Red bars in an uptrend mean slowing, not falling.
  • Shrinking histogram peaks across successive pushes mean a maturing trend: be selective and defensive.
  • The hook — the first clearly shorter bar of a pullback — is an early cue, not an entry. Wait for a price trigger.
  • Hook entries are cheaper than crossover entries, allowing tighter stops and larger size at the same risk, at the cost of more false starts.
  • Outside pullbacks and new swing extremes, the histogram is mostly noise.

quiz.q: The histogram has been red for 30 candles while price has risen 150 pips. What is the best reading?
options: The uptrend continues but at a slower speed than earlier
quiz.why: Red bars above a positive MACD line mean speed is below its recent average. The trend can keep rising while decelerating.

quiz.q: What is the histogram hook?
options: The first histogram bar of a pullback that is clearly shorter than the one before it
A histogram bar that crosses zero
The tallest bar on the chart
A hand-drawn line on the histogram
quiz.why: The hook is the first contraction after the pullback's bars have been growing — an early sign the counter-move is losing force.

quiz.q: Why is a price trigger required after the hook?
options: Because a slowing decline can continue falling; the trigger shows buyers have actually taken control for a candle
quiz.why: The hook only shows slowing. A close above the prior candle's high is evidence that price has actually turned.

quiz.q: In 'The hook: earlier than the crossover', how much cheaper was the hook entry than the signal-line cross?
quiz.why: Hook entry at 111 versus the crossover close about 31 pips higher — which also allowed a much tighter stop.

quiz.q: Three successive pushes make higher highs with smaller and smaller histogram clusters. What should a trend trader do?
options: Treat the trend as maturing: be more selective with new longs and protect open profits
Ignore it — histogram height has no meaning
quiz.why: Shrinking pushes signal fading acceleration. Structure is still bullish, so the right response is defensive, not reversal.

quiz.q: An impulse rose 140 pips in 20 candles. The pullback has fallen 60 pips in 5 candles and the histogram has just hooked. How should you treat the setup?
options: As a strong buy — the hook is early
With caution or not at all — the pullback is travelling faster per candle than the impulse did
Wait for the zero-line cross before buying
quiz.why: Twelve pips per candle against seven: the counter-move is more forceful than the trend. That is the profile of a pullback that may become a reversal.

lessons.title: MACD Divergence Without the Myths
lessons.summary: Identify genuine MACD divergence, understand why it happens, and trade it only after price structure confirms — while recognising the strong trends where divergence repeats and fails.
lessons.html:
Divergence is the most romanticised idea in technical analysis. Price makes a new high, the indicator does not, and a story is born: the move is "running out of steam", "smart money is distributing", "a reversal is imminent". Screenshots of divergences that preceded big turns are shared endlessly. Screenshots of divergences that preceded another 300 pips of trend are not.

This lesson treats divergence for what it actually is: a measurement. You already know from Lesson 1 that the MACD line is a speed reading. Divergence is simply what you see when price keeps making progress while that speed reading falls. It is real information, and it is useful — but it is a warning, not a trigger, and in a strong trend it can repeat several times before anything happens.

What divergence is

There are two classic forms:

  • Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high, but the MACD line makes a lower high at the same time.
  • Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low, but the MACD line makes a higher low.

Use the MACD line, not the histogram, for this. The histogram is noisier and produces divergences constantly. The line is smoother and its peaks correspond more closely to the swings you can see on price.

In speed terms, bearish divergence says: "The second push to a new high was slower than the first." Nothing more. The market is still going up — it made a new high — but it got there with less urgency. That might be the first sign of a trend ending. It might also be a trend settling from a sprint into a jog, as the 'Speed peaks before price does' chart in Lesson 1 showed.

Look carefully at the sequence in that chart. The divergence was visible at the second peak, but the trade did not happen there. It happened about eighteen candles later, after price itself had done two things: made a lower high, and broken the swing low beneath it. By then the divergence was no longer a theory about slowing momentum. It was a slowing trend that had also changed structure.

KEY POINT

Divergence is a warning, not an entry. Price structure — a lower high and a break of the low beneath it — is the confirmation.

The confirmation rule

For a bearish divergence trade, the full sequence is:

  1. Divergence: price makes a higher high; the MACD line makes a lower high. Draw the line between the two peaks on both price and indicator.
  2. First drop: price falls from the second peak and forms a swing low.
  3. Lower high: price bounces but fails below the second peak.
  4. Trigger: a candle closes below the swing low from step 2. Enter on that close.
  5. Stop: above the lower high from step 3.
  6. Target: at least 2R, or the next significant support if it offers at least 1.5R.

Mirror every step for a bullish divergence. Some traders will think this is too slow, and they are right that it gives away part of the move. What it buys in return is that every trade you take has already shown the two things a reversal needs: lost momentum and changed structure. You also get a logical place for the stop, which a raw divergence entry does not give you.

The bullish example has the same shape upside down. Note the stop distance: 28 pips, because the higher low gave a nearby, logical place for it. Compare that with buying at the second low on divergence alone, where the only possible stop is "somewhere below the low" — and where, if the low breaks, you have no idea how far it might run.

When divergence fails

Here is the chart that the divergence screenshots never show. Strong trends decelerate in stages, and every stage can produce a divergence.

This is why the confirmation rule matters. The trader who sold on divergence alone was wrong twice — and in a real market, could have been wrong three or four times. The trader who waited for structure was never in the trade at all, because the structure never changed. Their divergence observations were still useful: they told them the trend was maturing, which is a reason to tighten management of existing longs. They just were not a reason to sell.

COMMON MISTAKE

Selling every bearish divergence in an uptrend. In strong trends divergence repeats, because speed naturally falls from its early peak. Without a lower high and a broken swing low, there is no reversal to trade.

Practice drill

The chart below stops shortly after a clear bearish divergence. Price has started to drop. Decide whether there is a trade before you reveal.

Line or histogram?

You will see divergence drawn on the histogram as often as on the MACD line, and the two can disagree. The histogram compares the MACD line with its own recent average, so it peaks earlier and more often; almost every second push in any trend produces a smaller histogram cluster, as Lesson 5 showed. That makes histogram divergence common and individually weak. The MACD line moves more slowly, and its peaks line up better with the swings you can see on price. For the confirmation rule in this lesson, use the line. If you also notice histogram divergence, treat it as background colour, not as a second, independent warning — both are built from the same averages, so two of them do not double the evidence.

Why divergence happens — honestly

You will read that divergence shows "smart money quietly selling into strength" or "institutions distributing". Perhaps sometimes. But the chart cannot show you anyone's intentions. What the chart shows is narrower and more reliable: the second push covered less distance per candle than the first. The MACD line, being a speed reading, fell.

There are dull and perfectly healthy reasons for that. Trends often start with a sharp repricing and settle into a steadier pace. A second push may happen in a quieter session. The first push may have been inflated by a news candle — the 'One candle, the biggest reading on the chart' example in Lesson 3 is a divergence waiting to happen. Price first. Indicator second. Stories, if at all, last.

Going deeper

Choosing the right peaks. Divergence must compare price swings with the MACD readings at those swings. Draw it between two clear swing highs on price, then check the MACD line at those same candles (or within a candle or two). Comparing a price high with an unrelated MACD peak several candles away is a common way to see divergences that are not there. The best divergences are between swings that are clearly separated — at least 10 to 15 candles apart — with the MACD line having pulled back meaningfully towards its signal line or zero between them.

Hidden divergence. The reverse pattern — price makes a higher low while the MACD line makes a lower low — is called hidden bullish divergence. It means a pullback pushed the speed reading lower than the previous pullback did, yet price held a higher low. Some traders treat this as a continuation signal in an uptrend. It is less reliable than the textbook claims suggest, and it overlaps heavily with the pullback methods in Lesson 7. Treat it as supporting evidence for a with-trend setup, not as a setup by itself.

Divergence and the zero line. Bearish divergences that form while the MACD line stays high above zero are weaker warnings than those that form after the line has already fallen back to zero between the peaks. In the second case, the market has already shown a full loss of trend speed once; the second peak is a recovery that failed to match the first.

Expectancy, illustratively. Suppose, hypothetically, that confirmed divergence trades reached 2R slightly less than half the time and stopped out at −1R the rest. The expectancy would be positive but modest, and the strategy would regularly produce runs of several losses. These numbers are invented to show the shape of the maths, not a claim about how any method performs. The real figures for your market can only come from your own testing.

Multiple timeframes. A divergence on a lower timeframe inside a strong higher-timeframe trend is usually just the end of a pullback or a push within that trend. Divergences that line up with a higher-timeframe level — a prior major high, a weekly range edge — carry more weight. Even then, the confirmation rule stays the same.

Summary

  • Bearish divergence: higher high on price, lower high on the MACD line. Bullish: lower low on price, higher low on the MACD line.
  • Divergence means the second push was slower. It is a warning of a maturing move, not a reversal signal.
  • Trade it only after confirmation: a lower high (or higher low) and a close through the swing between.
  • Strong trends produce repeated divergences. Without structural change, do not fade them.
  • Charts show speed and structure, not intentions. Price first, indicator second.

quiz.q: Which describes bearish MACD divergence?
options: Lower high on price, higher high on MACD
Higher high on price, lower high on the MACD line
Histogram turns red at a new high
quiz.why: Bearish divergence is price making a higher high while the MACD line makes a lower high.

quiz.q: In speed terms, what does bearish divergence tell you?
options: The second push to a new high was slower than the first
quiz.why: The MACD line is a speed reading. Lower peaks mean the later push covered less distance per candle — nothing more.

quiz.q: Under this lesson's confirmation rule, when is a bearish divergence short entered?
options: On a close below the swing low that formed after the second peak, once a lower high is in place
When the MACD line crosses zero
quiz.why: The rule requires the divergence, a lower high, and a close through the swing low between — structure confirms the warning.

quiz.q: In 'Two divergences, no reversal', why did the confirmation rule keep the trader out?
options: Price never made a lower high or broke a swing low
The MACD line was below zero
quiz.why: Without structural change, the rule never triggers, no matter how many divergences appear.

quiz.q: Where does the stop go on a confirmed bullish divergence long?
options: Below the higher low that formed after the second price low
There is no stop on divergence trades
quiz.why: The higher low is the structure the trade depends on. If it breaks, the reversal idea is wrong.

quiz.q: A trader compares a price high with a MACD peak seven candles earlier and calls it divergence. What is wrong?
options: Divergence must compare the MACD readings at the same swings as the price highs
Divergence only works on daily charts
quiz.why: Mismatched peaks produce divergences that are not real. Compare the indicator at the same candles as the price swings.

lessons.title: The MACD Reset Pullback
lessons.summary: Trade with-trend pullbacks to the 20–50 EMA zone using the MACD reset towards zero, the histogram hook and a price trigger — with exact rules for entry, stop, target and when to skip.
lessons.html:
Everything so far has been preparation. You know MACD measures speed (Lesson 1), that crossovers are late (Lesson 2), that the zero line tells you which side to trade (Lesson 4), and that the histogram hook marks the moment a counter-move stops gaining force (Lesson 5). This lesson puts those pieces together into one complete, rule-based method.

The idea is simple. Strong trends do not move in straight lines. They surge, pause, pull back, and surge again. The best place to join a trend is not during the surge — when MACD is high, the crossover is long gone and the stop would be miles away — but at the end of a pullback, when the trend has cooled off, price is back near its averages and the next surge has not yet begun. MACD is unusually good at showing that cooling-off. We will call it the reset.

The reset: what cooling off looks like

During an impulse, the MACD line climbs to a peak: the trend is fast. During the pullback that follows, the 12 EMA drifts back towards the 26 EMA and the MACD line falls back towards zero. When it gets close to zero without breaking through, the trend's short-term speed has been fully "spent" — yet the longer averages still slope upward and price is still above them. That combination is what a healthy pause looks like.

The reset solves two problems at once. It answers "has the pullback gone far enough?" — the speed built up in the impulse has been fully given back. And it answers "is the trend still alive?" — the MACD line did not cross zero, so the 12 EMA is still above the 26 EMA. A pullback that has not reset is probably not finished. A pullback that drives the MACD line deep below zero is probably not a pullback.

KEY POINT

The best pullback longs come after the MACD line has fallen back towards zero but not through it. Speed is spent; the trend is intact.

The complete rules

Here is the method for longs. Mirror everything for shorts.

1. Trend. Price is above the 50 EMA, the 20 EMA is above the 50 EMA, and both slope upward. The impulse before the pullback drove the MACD line to a clear positive peak.

2. Pullback. Price pulls back into the zone between the 20 and 50 EMAs. A wick below the 50 EMA is acceptable; a close below it cancels the setup.

3. Reset. The MACD line has fallen to less than half of its impulse peak and is still above zero.

4. Hook. The histogram prints its first clearly shorter red bar.

5. Trigger. Within three candles of the hook, a candle closes above the high of the previous candle. Enter at that close.

6. Stop. A few pips below the pullback's lowest low.

7. Target. 2R, or the prior swing high if it is closer and still at least 1.5R away. If the prior high gives less than 1.5R, skip the trade.

8. Risk. A fixed fraction of the account per trade — 0.5% to 1% is a common illustrative range. Position size is that risk divided by the stop distance.

THE RULES
  • Longs only when price is above a rising 50 EMA, with the 20 EMA above the 50 EMA (mirror for shorts)
  • The pullback must reach the 20–50 EMA zone; a close beyond the 50 EMA cancels the setup
  • The MACD line must have reset to below half its impulse peak while staying above zero
  • Entry only on a price trigger (close beyond the previous candle's extreme) within three candles of a histogram hook
  • Stop beyond the pullback extreme; target 2R or the prior swing if it offers at least 1.5R
  • Risk a fixed fraction of the account; size = risk ÷ stop distance

Why the trigger must be a price candle

It is tempting to drop step five and enter on the hook itself, a few pips earlier. Resist it. The hook tells you the pullback has stopped accelerating; it does not tell you the pullback has stopped. Plenty of pullbacks slow, pause for a candle or two and then take another leg lower — the hook prints, the histogram even shrinks for a while, and price keeps falling. A close above the previous candle's high is different in kind. It is the first piece of evidence from price itself that buyers have taken control, however briefly. It also gives you a clean, objective entry that anyone could reproduce on the same chart. MACD tells you when to start watching. Price tells you when to act.

A winning trade

Step through it with the rules in hand. Trend: price above both EMAs, stacked and rising. Pullback: into the zone, no close below the 50 EMA. Reset: the MACD line fell from about 34 at the peak to under 4 — well below half — and never crossed zero. Hook: the histogram's red bars peaked and began shrinking. Trigger: a strong candle closed above the previous candle's high. Every condition was met, so the trade was taken. With 19 pips of risk at an illustrative 1% per trade, the target paid 2%.

A trade that should have been skipped

The rules exist mostly for the trades they refuse. Here is a pullback that looks inviting — a big rally, a sharp dip, a strong bounce — but breaks two rules before any trigger appears.

Notice how convincing the bounce was. The histogram turned green, the MACD line curled up, candles were large and bullish. A trader without rules might have bought it. The rules had already answered the question: once price closed below the 50 EMA and the MACD line went through zero, this was no longer a pullback in an uptrend. It was something else, and the method does not trade something else.

COMMON MISTAKE

Re-qualifying a cancelled setup because the bounce looks strong. Once the 50 EMA close or the MACD zero-line rule is broken, the setup is gone. A new trend has to build its own structure first.

A valid trade that lost

Rules do not make losing trades disappear. They make them small and affordable. This one met every condition and still failed.

Could anything have warned you? Honestly, not much. The bounce stalled under the midpoint of the prior impulse and the MACD line barely turned up — but those observations are clearer in hindsight than they were at the time. This is the trade every method produces, and the reason risk per trade must be small and fixed. Over a series of trades, a method like this only needs its winners to be large enough and frequent enough to outweigh losses like this one. Whether they are, on your market and timeframe, is a question only your own testing can answer.

The short side

The method is symmetrical. In a downtrend, price below a falling 50 EMA, the MACD line has made a clear negative trough; the pullback rallies into the 20–50 EMA zone; the MACD line rises back towards zero without crossing it; the histogram hooks; a candle closes below the previous candle's low.

Going deeper

Why the 20–50 EMA zone. The zone is a practical compromise. Pullbacks in strong trends often stop near the 20 EMA; pullbacks in steadier trends often reach the 50. Requiring the 20 alone would miss the deeper ones; requiring the 50 alone would miss the strongest trends entirely. The 50 EMA close rule is what separates "deep pullback" from "trend failure".

The half-peak reset threshold. The rule that the MACD line must fall below half its impulse peak is deliberately loose. Its purpose is to stop you buying a shallow dip while the trend is still very extended. If you test the method, try thresholds of a third and two-thirds as well. If results change dramatically between them, the method is fragile on that market. Robust methods tolerate sensible variation in their thresholds.

Higher-timeframe alignment. A refinement many traders use: only take trading-timeframe setups when the next timeframe up also has its MACD line above zero (for longs). In a variant of this method, when the higher-timeframe MACD is strongly positive, the trading-timeframe MACD line may be allowed to dip slightly below zero during the pullback. Choose one version, write it down and test it; mixing them trade by trade turns rules into opinions.

Trade management. The rules above use a fixed 2R target. Alternatives include taking half off at 1R and trailing the remainder below each new higher low, or exiting on a close below the 20 EMA. Each changes the shape of the results: fixed targets give more consistent outcomes; trailing exits occasionally catch large trends but give back more on average. There is no universally correct choice, only one that you test and apply consistently.

What breaks the method. Ranges (Lesson 8) and the late stage of trends, where pullbacks deepen and pushes shorten (Lesson 5). If three consecutive setups on a market fail, check whether the market is still trending at all before taking a fourth.

Summary

  • The reset: during a pullback the MACD line falls back towards zero without crossing it — speed spent, trend intact.
  • Rules: trend, pullback into the 20–50 EMA zone, reset below half the impulse peak, histogram hook, price trigger, stop beyond the pullback extreme, 2R target.
  • A close beyond the 50 EMA or the MACD line through zero cancels the setup, however strong the bounce looks.
  • Valid setups still lose. Fixed, small risk makes those losses affordable.
  • The method is symmetrical for shorts.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Price above a rising 50 EMA, 20 EMA above the 50 (mirror for shorts)
  • The impulse drove the MACD line to a clear peak
  • Pullback has reached the 20–50 EMA zone with no close beyond the 50 EMA
  • MACD line has reset below half its impulse peak and is still on the trend side of zero
  • Histogram has hooked
  • Trigger candle has closed beyond the previous candle's extreme within three candles of the hook
  • Stop placed beyond the pullback extreme; target at 2R or prior swing (minimum 1.5R)
  • Position sized so the stop equals the planned fixed risk

quiz.q: What is the MACD 'reset' in this method?
options: The MACD line falling back towards zero during a pullback without crossing it
Resetting the indicator settings to default
quiz.why: The reset is speed being spent during the pullback while the 12 EMA stays above the 26 EMA.

quiz.q: During a long setup, price closes below the 50 EMA but then bounces strongly with a histogram hook. What do the rules say?
options: Take the trade — the hook confirms it
The setup was cancelled by the close below the 50 EMA; no trade
Wait for the MACD zero cross and then buy
quiz.why: A close beyond the 50 EMA cancels the setup. A strong bounce does not re-qualify it.

quiz.q: The impulse took the MACD line to +40. During the pullback it has fallen to +28. Has it reset?
options: No — it has not yet fallen below half its peak (+20)
Yes, because it is above zero
Only if the histogram is red
quiz.why: The reset rule requires the MACD line to fall below half its impulse peak while staying above zero.

quiz.q: Where does the stop go on a reset pullback long?
options: A few pips below the pullback's lowest low
quiz.why: The pullback low is the structure the trade depends on. If price breaks it, the pullback has become something else.

quiz.q: The prior swing high offers only 1.1R from your planned entry. What do the rules say?
options: Take the trade with a 2R target anyway
Skip — the target must offer at least 1.5R
Move the stop closer to make it 2R
quiz.why: If the nearest obstacle gives less than 1.5R, the reward does not justify the risk. Moving the stop to fix the maths is not allowed.

quiz.q: In 'Valid setup, stopped out', what was the correct response to the loss?
options: Accept it — a valid setup lost 1R, which is part of any method
Re-enter immediately at a lower price
quiz.why: Every method has valid losing trades. Fixed, small risk keeps them affordable. Rules are judged over many trades, not one.

lessons.title: MACD in Ranges — Where It Whipsaws
lessons.summary: Recognise the sideways conditions that turn MACD into a whipsaw machine, switch your trend methods off in time, and use the histogram hook carefully at range edges instead.
lessons.html:
Every trend tool has a natural enemy, and for MACD it is the sideways market. In a trend, MACD's lag is a manageable cost. In a range, it is fatal. The averages wind around each other, the MACD line oscillates around zero, and every crossover arrives just as price reaches the opposite side of the range. A crossover trader in a range is a person who buys every high and sells every low, perfectly, on schedule.

Markets spend a large share of their time going sideways — on many pairs and timeframes, more time than they spend trending. So this is not a footnote. Recognising a range early is worth more to a MACD trader than any refinement to their entry rules. This lesson shows you what a range does to MACD, the symptoms that tell you to switch your trend methods off, and a cautious way to use the histogram at range edges instead.

What a range does to MACD, mechanically

In a range, price returns to the same levels again and again. The 12 and 26 EMAs both settle near the middle of the range, so their difference — the MACD line — hovers around zero. Each swing from one side of the range to the other pushes the MACD line a little above zero, then a little below.

Now add the lag from Lesson 2. A swing from the bottom of the range to the top takes, say, eight candles. A signal-line crossover needs several candles to confirm. By the time a bullish crossover prints, the swing is half over. By the time the bearish crossover follows, price has already turned down from the top and is heading back to the middle. The result is a machine that buys in the middle on the way up and sells in the middle on the way down.

Look at the timing. Each crossover is perfectly correct about the swing that has just happened — and each arrives too late to profit from it. There is nothing wrong with the indicator. It is measuring speed in a market where speed reverses every eight candles, which is roughly the delay the indicator needs to confirm anything.

KEY POINT

In a range, MACD's lag is about as long as the swings themselves, so every crossover arrives just in time to be wrong.

The symptoms: how to know you are in a range

You rarely know a range has started until it is a few swings old. The aim is to notice by the second or third swing, not the seventh. Four symptoms, in rough order of how early they appear:

  1. MACD peaks shrink towards zero. As a trend fades into a range, each swing produces a smaller MACD peak, until the line is oscillating in a narrow band around zero.
  2. The MACD line crosses zero repeatedly. Three or more zero-line crosses in the last 50 candles is a practical alarm.
  3. The 50 EMA flattens and price starts crossing it in both directions.
  4. Price swings repeat between the same levels. Highs fail at a similar price; lows hold at a similar price.

When you see these symptoms, the reset pullback method from Lesson 7 must be switched off. The reset depends on an impulse that drove the MACD line to a clear peak; in a range there is no such impulse, so there is nothing to reset from.
