A dip towards the 20 EMA in a range is not a pullback. It is just the next swing.

COMMON MISTAKE

Reading a range as "a trend with deep pullbacks" and continuing to take trend setups. If the MACD line is crossing zero every few swings, the trend method has nothing to work with.

What to do while you wait

Switching the trend methods off does not mean switching the screen off. A range is the setup period for the next trend, and there are useful jobs to do. Mark the range edges clearly and note how many touches each has had. Watch the MACD band around zero: a band that is narrowing often precedes a break. Check the higher timeframe, because a range on H1 is frequently just a pause inside an H4 trend, and the H4 MACD will tell you which edge is more likely to give way. Above all, decide in advance what a break would look like — a close beyond the edge, the MACD line leaving its band — so that when it happens you recognise the new regime instead of arguing with it.

The range-edge hook

There is a way to use MACD in a well-defined range, but it is a different method with different rules, and it is more fragile than the trend method. The idea: instead of using the histogram hook to time the end of a pullback in a trend, use it to time the end of a swing into the edge of a range.

The rules for a long at the range floor (mirror for shorts at the top):

  1. The range is established: at least two touches of both the floor and the top, and the range symptoms above are present.
  2. Price swings down into the floor zone.
  3. The histogram hooks (first clearly shorter red bar).
  4. A candle closes above the previous candle's high, inside or just above the floor zone.
  5. Stop a few pips below the floor zone.
  6. Target 2R or the middle of the range, whichever is nearer — but skip the trade if the range midpoint offers less than 1.5R.

Ranges end, and when they end they usually end through one of the edges you are trading from. That makes the range-edge hook a method with a built-in failure mode: the breakout. The stop below the floor is what keeps that failure affordable.

The losing trade carries useful information. When a range breaks, the MACD line typically leaves its narrow band around zero and moves decisively to one side. That is the first sign that a new trend is forming. The trend method does not fire immediately — it needs an impulse peak and then a pullback reset — but the range method should now be switched off.

Practice drill

This market was trending. Price has just bounced off a dip towards the 50 EMA and a candle has closed above the previous high, with the histogram contracting. Would you take a Lesson 7 reset long?

Going deeper

Why ranges are so common. Trends need a persistent imbalance — new information, flows that keep arriving in one direction. Most of the time, neither side has that edge, and price oscillates around a level that both sides find acceptable. On lower timeframes especially, ranges and choppy, overlapping price action can dominate. A trend method that sits out these periods is not missing opportunities; it is avoiding the conditions in which it has no edge.

A quantitative range filter. If you prefer a rule to judgement, combine two measures. First, count MACD zero-line crosses over the last 50 candles; three or more is a warning. Second, measure the 50 EMA's slope: the change in the 50 EMA over the last 20 candles, divided by the average candle range over the same period. When that ratio is small — for example below about 1 — the average is effectively flat. These thresholds are starting points for testing, not truths.

Range-edge versus trend method: different statistics. Range-edge trades tend to have smaller targets, because a range has a ceiling. They also fail by breakout, which tends to happen suddenly. Treat them as a separate method with its own journal, its own results and its own risk setting — many traders use half their normal risk on range trades. Do not let a run of range wins change how you trade trends, or vice versa.

Transitions are the hardest part. The most expensive moments are the two transitions: trend into range (when trend setups keep failing) and range into trend (when range-edge trades get run over). The symptom lists are your defence. A practical habit: after two consecutive losses with either method, stop and re-classify the market from scratch before the next trade.

Volatility compression. Ranges often narrow before they break. If the range's swings are getting smaller and the MACD band around zero is getting tighter, the breakout may be close. That is a reason to stop taking range-edge trades, not to guess the breakout direction.

Summary

  • In a range the MACD line hovers around zero and crossovers arrive just as each swing ends — a whipsaw machine.
  • Symptoms: shrinking MACD peaks, repeated zero-line crosses, a flat 50 EMA, repeated swing levels.
  • When the symptoms appear, switch the trend methods off. There is no impulse to reset from.
  • The range-edge hook can work in an established range, with a stop beyond the edge and a modest target.
  • Ranges end through their edges. A MACD line that leaves its band around zero is the first sign of a new trend.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • At least two touches of both range edges
  • Range symptoms present: MACD hugging zero, repeated zero crosses, flat 50 EMA
  • Price in the edge zone, histogram hooked, trigger candle closed back inside
  • Stop beyond the edge zone; target 2R or range midpoint (minimum 1.5R)
  • Reduced risk compared with trend trades, if that is your plan

quiz.q: Why do MACD crossovers perform so badly in ranges?
options: The indicator's confirmation delay is about as long as each swing, so signals arrive as swings end
MACD is not calculated in ranges
quiz.why: Each crossover needs several candles to confirm; in a range that is about half the swing, so buys print mid-rally and sells mid-decline.

quiz.q: Which is the earliest typical symptom of a trend fading into a range?
options: MACD peaks shrinking towards zero with each swing
quiz.why: Shrinking MACD swings usually appear first, before the 50 EMA has fully flattened and before many zero crosses have accumulated.

quiz.q: The MACD line has crossed zero four times in the last 40 candles and the 50 EMA is flat. A dip reaches the 20 EMA with a histogram hook. Take a Lesson 7 reset long?
options: Yes, every condition for a hook is met
No — the trend method is switched off in a range; there is no impulse to reset from
Only if it is the London session
quiz.why: Range symptoms are present. The reset method depends on a trend impulse, which does not exist here.

quiz.q: Where does the stop go on a range-edge long at the floor?
options: A few pips below the floor zone
No stop is needed in a range
quiz.why: The range floor is the structure the trade depends on. If it breaks, the range has ended.

quiz.q: After a range-edge long is stopped out, the MACD line moves well below zero and stays there. What does that suggest?
options: The range is intact; buy again
The range has likely broken into a new downtrend; switch off range trades
quiz.why: Leaving the narrow band around zero decisively is the first sign of a new trend. Range methods should be switched off.

quiz.q: In 'Seven crossover trades, seven losses', what was visible on the price chart all along?
options: A flat 50 EMA and repeated swing levels
quiz.why: The flat average and repeated highs and lows showed a range from early on — the cue to switch crossover trading off.

lessons.title: Practical MACD Rule Sets
lessons.summary: Classify the market regime first, choose the matching MACD rule set, align it with the higher timeframe, and manage risk and open trades with written rules you can test.
lessons.html:
You now have three MACD methods: the reset pullback for trends (Lesson 7), confirmed divergence for reversals (Lesson 6), and the range-edge hook for sideways markets (Lesson 8). Each one works in its own conditions and fails, sometimes badly, outside them. The single most common way traders destroy a sound method is not bad entries. It is using the right method in the wrong market.

This lesson turns the course into a working process. You will learn to classify the market before you look for any setup, choose the one rule set that fits, check it against the higher timeframe, and manage risk and open positions with rules rather than feelings. Nothing new is invented here. The value is in the order and the discipline.

Step one: classify the regime

Before you look at a single entry signal, answer one question: what kind of market is this? There are three answers, and each maps to one rule set.

  • Trending. Price above a rising 50 EMA (or below a falling one), swing structure stepping in one direction, the MACD line making clear peaks on the trend side of zero and rarely crossing it. Rule set A: reset pullback.
  • Ranging. Flat 50 EMA, repeated swing levels, the MACD line hugging zero and crossing it repeatedly. Rule set C: range-edge hook — or no trading at all, if you prefer.
  • Transitioning. A mature trend showing divergence and fading pushes, or a range starting to break. Rule set B: confirmed divergence, but only once structure confirms; until then, stand aside.

The unshaded gaps in that chart matter as much as the shaded areas. Between regimes there is a period when the old method has stopped working and the new one has not started. The correct action in that gap is usually nothing. A trader who is comfortable doing nothing for a while has a large advantage over one who needs a trade every session.

KEY POINT

Classify first, then choose the rule set. Never look for an entry before you have decided what kind of market you are in.

Step two: align with the higher timeframe

Lesson 3 introduced the principle: direction from the higher timeframe, timing from the lower one. In rule form, for rule set A:

  • Longs on the trading timeframe only when the next timeframe up (roughly four to six times longer) has its MACD line above zero.
  • Shorts only when it is below zero.
  • If the higher timeframe is in a range (MACD hugging zero), trade the trading timeframe as a range or stand aside.

Now the same H1 picture, but with the higher timeframe pointing the other way.

The second chart is the best argument for the alignment rule. Nothing on the H1 chart was wrong. Every condition of rule set A was met. The information that should have stopped the trade was simply not on that chart. That is why classification and alignment come before setups: they put the setup in context.

Step three: the rule sets, written down

Here are the three methods in compressed form. They are the rules from Lessons 6, 7 and 8, written as you might keep them on a card next to your screen.

THE RULES
  • A (Reset pullback, trending regime): higher-timeframe MACD on your side of zero; price beyond a sloping 50 EMA; pullback into the 20–50 EMA zone; MACD line reset below half its impulse peak without crossing zero; histogram hook; trigger close beyond previous candle; stop beyond pullback extreme; 2R target
  • B (Confirmed divergence, transition): divergence between two clear swings on the MACD line; a lower high (or higher low) forms; trigger on a close through the swing between; stop beyond that lower high (or higher low); 2R target or next level (minimum 1.5R)
  • C (Range-edge hook, ranging regime): two or more touches of each edge; range symptoms present; hook and trigger at the edge; stop beyond the edge zone; target 2R or range midpoint (minimum 1.5R); reduced risk
  • In every rule set: no trade without a stop placed at entry, and no stop moved further away once placed

Notice what is not on the card. There is no plain crossover method, because Lessons 2 and 8 showed it has no structural stop and no defence against ranges. There is no zero-line-cross entry, because it is too late. There is no "divergence alone" entry, because Lesson 6 showed how it fails in strong trends. Each of those ideas survives only as part of something else: the zero line as a filter, the crossover's cousin the hook as a timing cue, divergence as a warning.

Step four: risk rules

Entries decide whether a trade is good. Risk rules decide whether a bad run is survivable. The numbers below are illustrative starting points; choose your own and keep them fixed.

  • Risk per trade: a fixed fraction of the account, for example 0.5% to 1%. Position size = risk ÷ stop distance.
  • Correlated exposure: EUR/USD and GBP/USD longs are largely the same bet on a weaker US dollar. Treat correlated positions as one risk unit, or cap combined risk.
  • Daily and weekly limits: for example, stop for the day after losses totalling 2R, and for the week after 5R. This protects you from the most dangerous trader in the room — yourself after three losses.
  • No averaging down. Adding to a losing position turns a 1R loss into a much larger one.

Run the numbers on a losing streak, which every method has. With 1% risk per trade, eight consecutive losses take the account down by roughly 7.7%. With 3% risk per trade, the same streak costs about 22%. The method has not changed; only the sizing has. Runs of that length are not rare in any method with a modest strike rate, so size for them.

Step five: managing open trades

MACD has one more job once you are in a trend trade: telling you when to become defensive.

That is the correct use of divergence on an open position: not a reason to reverse, but a reason to protect. Two practical management rules:

  1. When a bearish divergence forms against an open long, take no new longs and trail the stop for any remaining position below the most recent higher low. Mirror for shorts.
  2. When the MACD line crosses zero against an open position that has not yet hit its target, exit. The trend filter has closed; the reason for the trade is gone.
COMMON MISTAKE

Changing the rules mid-trade. Moving a target further away because "momentum is strong", or a stop further away because "it's just a pullback", replaces a tested process with a feeling. Write the management rules before the trade and follow them.

Step six: test before you trust

Every rule in this course is a hypothesis about how a market behaves, not a fact. Before trading any rule set with real money, test it:

  1. Pick one market and one timeframe.
  2. Scroll back at least a few hundred candles. Hide the future (most platforms have a replay mode).
  3. Step forward a candle at a time. Classify the regime. When a setup appears, record entry, stop and target before you look further.
  4. Record every trade — winners, losers and the ones you skipped and why.
  5. After at least 50–100 trades, look at the results: average R per trade, longest losing streak, worst drawdown. Then decide whether the method deserves a small, live, demo-size trial.

Results from a careful manual test are still optimistic — you know the course's rules were written with hindsight, and live trading adds spreads, slippage and emotion. Treat any result as an upper bound, not a forecast.

Going deeper

Rules that a stranger could follow. A good test of your written rules is whether someone else could apply them to the same chart and reach the same decision. "Strong trend" fails that test; "price above a 50 EMA whose value is higher than 20 candles ago" passes it. Every place where your rules say "clear", "strong" or "good", either define it numerically or accept that you are using judgement and record it as such.

One method per regime, one change at a time. When results disappoint, change one rule, re-test, and compare. Changing three things at once makes it impossible to know which change helped. Keep a version history of your rules, with dates.

Expectancy, illustratively. A method's average result per trade is (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss). With 2R targets and 1R stops, a hypothetical method that wins 40% of the time averages 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = +0.2R per trade before costs; at 30% it averages −0.1R. These figures are invented to show the arithmetic, not to describe any real method. The point is how sensitive the outcome is to small changes in win rate, costs and average win — which is why testing matters.

When nothing fits. Some days no regime is clear. The market is neither trending cleanly nor ranging cleanly. The right rule set for those days is the empty one. Write that down too: "If I cannot classify the regime within two minutes, I do not trade it."

Summary

  • Classify the regime first: trending (set A), ranging (set C), transitioning (set B after confirmation, otherwise wait).
  • Align with the higher timeframe: its MACD zero line sets the permitted direction.
  • Keep the three rule sets written down; plain crossovers, zero-cross entries and unconfirmed divergence are not on the card.
  • Fix risk per trade, cap correlated exposure and set daily and weekly loss limits.
  • Use divergence to protect open trades, and exit when the MACD line crosses zero against you. Test everything before trusting it.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Regime classified: trending, ranging or transitioning (if unclear, no trade)
  • Rule set chosen to match the regime
  • Higher-timeframe MACD on the permitted side of zero (rule set A)
  • Every condition of the chosen rule set met, with no exceptions
  • Stop placed at entry; target at least 1.5R; position sized to fixed risk
  • Correlated exposure and daily loss limit checked
  • Management rules for divergence and zero-line exit written down before entry

quiz.q: What is the first step before looking for any MACD entry?
quiz.why: The regime decides which rule set applies. Entries found before classification are often the right method in the wrong market.

quiz.q: The H1 chart shows a perfect reset long, but the H4 MACD line is below zero. What does the alignment rule say?
options: Take it — the H1 setup is perfect
Skip it — the higher timeframe does not permit longs
Take it with a wider stop
quiz.why: Direction comes from the higher timeframe. An H1 uptrend inside an H4 downtrend is a counter-trend rally.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the course's rule sets?
quiz.why: Plain crossovers have no structural stop and whipsaw in ranges. They survive only as ideas inside other methods.

quiz.q: With 1% risk per trade, roughly how much does a run of eight consecutive losses cost?
quiz.why: Compounded: 1 − 0.99^8 ≈ 7.7%. At 3% per trade the same streak costs about 22%.

quiz.q: A bearish divergence forms while you hold part of a long position. What does the management rule say?
options: Take no new longs and trail the stop below the most recent higher low
quiz.why: Divergence is a reason to protect, not to reverse. Structure decides the exit.

quiz.q: Using the illustrative formula, what is the expectancy of a hypothetical method with a 40% win rate, 2R wins and 1R losses, before costs?
quiz.why: 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = 0.8 − 0.6 = +0.2R per trade. The figures are hypothetical, used to show the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Capstone: The Complete MACD Playbook
lessons.summary: Run the whole MACD process from regime to exit on three full worked trades, then use the strategy passport and pre-trade checklist to apply it on your own charts.
lessons.html:
This is the lesson to keep open next to your charts. It gathers everything from the course into one process — the playbook — and then walks through three complete trades from first glance to final exit: two that worked and one that did not. It finishes with the strategy passport, the full pre-trade checklist and a final drill.

Before you start, one reminder about what this playbook is. It is a structured way of using MACD that respects what the indicator actually measures: speed and acceleration, built from averages, always late. It is not a prediction machine and it does not remove losing trades. Its job is to make sure that every trade you take has a reason, a stop and a size you decided in advance, and that you stay out of the conditions where MACD has nothing useful to say.

The playbook, step by step

Step 1 — Read the higher timeframe. Open the timeframe four to six times above your trading chart. Is its MACD line above zero, below zero, or hugging it? This sets your permitted direction. Hugging zero means no trend trades.

Step 2 — Classify the regime on your trading timeframe. Trending: price beyond a sloping 50 EMA, clear MACD peaks on one side of zero. Ranging: flat 50 EMA, repeated swing levels, MACD crossing zero repeatedly. Transitioning: divergence and fading pushes at the end of a trend, or a range edge giving way. If you cannot classify it in two minutes, stop here.

Step 3 — Choose the rule set. Trending and aligned with the higher timeframe: rule set A, the reset pullback. Transitioning with a clear divergence: rule set B, but only after structure confirms. Ranging: rule set C, the range-edge hook, or no trade.

Step 4 — Wait for every condition. For rule set A: pullback into the 20–50 EMA zone without a close beyond the 50; MACD line reset below half its impulse peak without crossing zero; histogram hook; trigger candle within three candles of the hook. Missing one condition means no trade.

Step 5 — Place the stop, then size the position. Stop beyond the pullback extreme (A), the lower high or higher low (B), or the range edge (C). Position size = fixed risk ÷ stop distance.

Step 6 — Check the target. 2R, or the nearest obstacle if it offers at least 1.5R. Less than 1.5R: skip.

Step 7 — Manage by rule. Exit at the target or stop. If a divergence forms against an open position, take no new trades in that direction and trail any remainder beyond the latest swing. If the MACD line crosses zero against an unfinished trade, exit.

Step 8 — Record it. Regime, rule set, entry, stop, target, outcome in R, and one line about anything you would do differently.

Worked trade 1: a reset pullback long

Walk through the playbook.

Higher timeframe: the daily MACD line is above zero, so longs are permitted. Regime: on the H4 chart price is above a rising 50 EMA, the 20 EMA is above the 50, and the impulse drove the MACD line to a clear peak of about 37 — trending, so rule set A. Conditions: the pullback dropped through the zone between the 20 and 50 EMAs and one candle's wick pierced the 50 — but that candle closed just above it, so the setup survived. The MACD line fell to about 2: well under half its peak, still above zero. On the very next candle the histogram's red bar shrank — the hook — and the same candle closed far above the previous high: the trigger. Stop and size: the pullback's low sat at 106, so the stop went at 102, 26 pips away. At an illustrative 1% risk, that sets the size. Target: 2R at 180. The prior high at 188 was further away, so it did not limit the target. Outcome: the target was reached nine candles later: +2R.

Notice what the trader did not do. They did not buy during the impulse because MACD was "strong". They did not buy the first red histogram bar. They did not wait for the signal-line cross, which came six candles later and over 30 pips higher. And they did not panic when a wick poked through the 50 EMA: the rule is about closes, and the close held. Each of those choices is a lesson from earlier in the course.

Worked trade 2: a confirmed divergence short

Higher timeframe: the daily MACD line had been falling towards zero — the larger trend was losing speed, which is the context in which rule set B makes sense. Regime: a mature uptrend showing divergence: transitioning. Conditions: the divergence was clear — price's second peak was about 30 pips higher, the MACD line's second peak about half the height of the first. But the playbook says divergence is a warning, so the trader did nothing at the peak. Price fell to a swing low at 132, bounced to a lower high near 160 and then closed below 132. That close was the trigger. Stop and size: above the lower high, at 163: 33 pips. Target: 2R at 64. Outcome: reached: +2R.

The trade was taken roughly twenty candles after the divergence first appeared, and about 55 pips below the high. Someone who sold the high on divergence alone would have done better on this chart — and would have been run over on the 'Two divergences, no reversal' chart in Lesson 6. The confirmation rule gives up some trades' best prices in exchange for avoiding the worst ones.

Worked trade 3: a valid long that lost

Higher timeframe: up. Regime: trending. Conditions: all met — the MACD line reset from about 35 to under 2, never crossed zero, the histogram hooked and a strong candle closed above the previous high. Stop and size: below the pullback low, 20 pips. Outcome: price rallied 12 pips, stalled and broke down. Stopped out: −1R.

What should the trader do with this? Record it, and nothing else. They should not change the rules because of one loss, should not add a filter that happens to exclude this exact chart, and should not double the size on the next trade to "win it back". Over a long series of trades, the method is judged by its average outcome in R, which includes losses like this. Across these three trades the net result was +3R — but three trades prove nothing in either direction, and the next three could easily be three losses.

KEY POINT

A valid trade that loses is not a mistake. A mistake is a trade taken without every condition, a stop moved, or a position sized by feel.

The strategy passport

The whole course on one card.

  • Market: liquid major currency pairs and gold on H1 to D1, in a trending regime confirmed by the higher timeframe's MACD line.
  • Wait for: a pullback into the 20–50 EMA zone that resets the MACD line to below half its impulse peak without crossing zero.
  • Trigger: the first histogram hook, followed within three candles by a close beyond the previous candle's extreme.
  • Stop: a few pips beyond the pullback's extreme. Size the position so the stop equals your fixed risk.
  • Target: 2R, or the prior swing if closer and still at least 1.5R. Exit early if the MACD line crosses zero against you.
  • Avoid: ranges (MACD hugging zero, flat 50 EMA), counter-trend crossovers, unconfirmed divergence, single-candle news spikes and any setup that conflicts with the higher timeframe.

The full pre-trade checklist

PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Higher-timeframe MACD line on the permitted side of zero (not hugging it)
  • Regime classified on the trading timeframe; rule set chosen to match
  • Price beyond a sloping 50 EMA, with the 20 EMA on the same side (rule set A)
  • Impulse drove the MACD line to a clear peak; pullback has reset it below half that peak without crossing zero
  • Pullback reached the 20–50 EMA zone with no close beyond the 50 EMA
  • Histogram has hooked; trigger candle closed beyond the previous candle's extreme within three candles
  • Stop placed beyond the pullback extreme (or lower high / higher low for rule set B, range edge for C)
  • Target at 2R, or nearest obstacle if at least 1.5R; otherwise skip
  • Position size = fixed risk ÷ stop distance; correlated exposure and daily loss limit checked
  • No major scheduled news due before the trigger candle closes
  • Management plan written: divergence → protect; MACD zero-line cross against the trade → exit
THE RULES
  • No trade without a classified regime and a matching rule set
  • No trade against the higher-timeframe MACD zero line
  • No entry without a price trigger; MACD alone never triggers a trade
  • No trade without a stop placed at entry; never move a stop further away
  • Fixed risk per trade; no averaging down; stop trading for the day at the daily loss limit

Final drill

The chart stops on the close of a candle in a downtrend. Work through the playbook — every step — before you press reveal. Assume the higher-timeframe MACD line is below zero.

Going deeper

Building your own evidence. The worked trades in this course are training charts: illustrative, built to show the process clearly, not records of real market history. The only evidence that matters for your trading is the evidence you gather yourself. Run the step-by-step test from Lesson 9 on at least one market and timeframe, record at least 50 to 100 setups, and look honestly at the average R, the longest losing run and the deepest drawdown before risking money.

Adapting without breaking. You will want to adjust things: different targets, a trailing exit, a different EMA zone. That is fine, provided you change one thing at a time, test it, and keep the parts of the method that carry its logic — the regime classification, the higher-timeframe alignment, the price trigger and the structural stop. Those four are what turn MACD from a lagging line into a usable process.

What MACD will never do. It will never see support and resistance, never know about tomorrow's interest-rate decision and never tell you a move is about to start. Everything in this playbook is built around that honesty: price structure decides, MACD describes speed, and risk rules keep you in the game long enough for the process to matter.

Where to go next. The same speed-and-acceleration thinking applies to other momentum tools. RSI and the stochastic measure similar things on bounded scales; rate-of-change measures speed directly. If you understand why MACD behaves the way it does, you will understand them quickly — and you will be just as sceptical of their "signals".

Summary

  • The playbook: higher timeframe, regime, rule set, every condition, stop then size, target check, rule-based management, record.
  • Trade 1 (reset long) and trade 2 (confirmed divergence short) each returned +2R; trade 3, equally valid, lost 1R.
  • A valid loss is not a mistake; broken rules are.
  • The passport and checklist summarise the whole course for daily use.
  • Evidence comes from your own testing. Training charts teach the process; they do not prove a result.

quiz.q: What is step 1 of the playbook?
options: Read the higher timeframe's MACD line to set the permitted direction
quiz.why: Direction comes first from the higher timeframe. Everything else is filtered through it.

quiz.q: In Trade 1, why did the trader not wait for the signal-line crossover?
options: The hook plus price trigger came earlier, giving a cheaper entry and tighter stop; the crossover came over 30 pips higher
The platform did not show it
quiz.why: The method uses the hook and a price trigger; the later crossover would have meant a worse entry and a wider stop.

quiz.q: In Trade 2, when was the short entered?
options: At the second peak, on divergence
On the first red histogram bar
On the close below the swing low after a lower high had formed
When the MACD line crossed zero
quiz.why: Rule set B requires divergence, then a lower high, then a close through the swing low between.

quiz.q: After Trade 3 lost 1R with every condition met, what is the correct response?
options: Add a filter that would have excluded this chart
Record it and keep following the rules
quiz.why: A valid loss is part of any method. Changing rules after one trade, or sizing up to recover, replaces process with emotion.

quiz.q: According to the passport, which is on the 'avoid' list?
quiz.why: Ranges defeat MACD's trend methods. The passport lists them, counter-trend crossovers, unconfirmed divergence and higher-timeframe conflict under 'avoid'.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mistake rather than an acceptable loss?
options: A valid setup that hits its stop
A trade taken with the higher-timeframe MACD line on the wrong side of zero
Skipping a trade with only 1.2R to the prior high
quiz.why: Taking a trade that breaks the alignment rule is a process error, regardless of outcome.
